cue: How do you say someone always looks on the bright side?

es.literal: to see the glass half full
es.meaning: To take the optimistic view of a situation.
es.example: Perdimos el cliente, pero ella ve el vaso medio lleno: dice que aprendimos más en tres meses que en dos años.
es.exampleTranslation: We lost the client, but she sees the glass half full — she says we learned more in three months than in two years.

it.literal: to see the glass half full
it.meaning: To take the optimistic view of a situation.
it.example: Ha perso il treno e vede il bicchiere mezzo pieno: dice che così visita il museo.
it.exampleTranslation: He missed his train and sees the glass half full — says now he gets to visit the museum.

bridge.note: The same glass, the same half, the same optimism — and a false friend sitting in the middle of it. Spanish holds a vaso. Italian has that word too, vaso, and it means a vase or a jar: something you put flowers or preserves in, not something you drink from. Italian's drinking glass is a bicchiere. So the one word a Spanish speaker would never think to check is the one word that has to change.

interference.es_to_it: 'Il vaso mezzo pieno' describes a half-full flower vase. Italian needs bicchiere. This is worth learning beyond the idiom: Spanish vaso and Italian vaso are false friends everywhere, not just here.
interference.it_to_es: Spanish does not use a bicchiere-shaped word at all here — the glass is a vaso, and 'copa' would move it to a wine glass. SEE ALSO 0266, the pessimist's version of this entry, and 0267, which puts the same false friend inside a different idiom.
